name: Favourite-longshot bias
statement: In racetrack betting, money staked on horses at long odds returns less per unit than money staked on favourites, and the gap holds across millions of starts.
meaning: The claim is about rates of return by odds group, not about which horse wins. Longshots lose more often than favourites by definition, and that is not the finding. The finding is that a pound placed on a 100/1 horse comes back smaller, on average, than a pound placed on the favourite, once every bet at each odds level is counted. Odds are prices, set by the pool in parimutuel betting and by bookmakers elsewhere, so the measured object is a market price rather than anything one bettor did. Two readings of the same curve have competed since the start. One says bettors like risk and pay for it. The other says bettors misperceive small and large probabilities, overweighting the first and underweighting the second. On win-bet data alone the two are observationally equivalent, because either a risk-loving utility function or a nonlinear probability weight can be fitted to the same declining returns. Separating them needs a wider choice set than win bets.

origin.note: "Odds Adjustments by American Horse-Race Bettors" tallied winners and entries at each odds level for 519 races from the 1947 spring meets at Churchill Downs, Belmont and Hialeah. It added selected odds groups from 867 further races over the first eight days of August 1947, weighted to represent 1,386 races. Griffith computed the average take as 13 percent and the average field as nine horses. After correcting the posted odds for take and breakage, the product of winners and odds exceeded the number of entries at short odds and fell below it at long odds. Linear interpolation put the crossover at odds of 6.1, a probability of 0.16. He framed the exercise as a field test of Preston and Baratta's laboratory finding that people overvalue small probabilities and undervalue large ones, and used neither the name the effect now carries nor a rate-of-return table.

evidence: The modern statement of the pattern comes from Snowberg and Wolfers, who obtained Jockey Club records of every horse start run in North America from 1992 to 2001. The primary sample is 6,403,712 starts in 865,934 races, reduced by their cleaning rules to 5,606,336 win-bet observations from 678,729 races. The rate of return on horses at odds of 100/1 or longer is about minus 61 percent. Betting at random returns about minus 23 percent, which is the track take. Betting the favourite in every race loses 5.5 percent. Between 4/1 and 9/1 the return is close to flat at minus 18 percent. The same shape appears in 2,725,000 starts in Australia and 380,000 starts in Great Britain, where odds are set by bookmakers rather than by a pool, so the pattern is not an artefact of parimutuel pricing. Snowberg and Wolfers then used compound bets to separate the two explanations. Exactas, quinellas and trifectas price combinations of the same horses, so a theory fitted to win bets makes a testable prediction about them. On 197,551 exactas the misperceptions class was closer to the actual price in 57.9 percent of cases against 42.1 percent for risk-love, and its mean absolute percentage error was 28.0 against 34.3. On 137,756 trifectas the split was 71.1 against 28.9, with errors of 57.4 percent against 100 percent. Relaxing the conditional-independence assumption behind those predictions changed little.

replication.headline: The pattern is close to settled in horse racing, where it reappears in samples of millions across three countries and both pricing systems, and it reverses in betting markets with only two outcomes.
replication.detail: The horse-racing record is unusually strong for this site, because the repeats are not fresh volunteers but the settled results of races people bet their own money on. Snowberg and Wolfers describe their data as an order of magnitude larger than any set previously examined and report that the bias has been stable since Griffith. They name the exceptions in the racing literature as Busche and Hall, on 2,653 Hong Kong races, and Busche, on a further 2,690 Hong Kong races and 1,738 Japanese races, both of which failed to find the bias. Neither of those papers was obtainable during this check, so the description of them here is Snowberg and Wolfers' rather than this site's reading. The reversals outside racing are documented in their own right. Woodland and Woodland examined the legal gambling market for major league baseball and report in their abstract that the racetrack bias runs in reverse there, with the deviations too small to fund a profitable strategy after commission. Their 2003 update adds the 1990 to 1999 seasons and reports the strength of the reverse bias as virtually identical, which they read as evidence that it is permanent. Their hockey work found a reverse bias strong enough to permit profitable wagering, and a later analysis of ten more seasons found it sustained for three and gone for the last seven as the market converged to efficiency. Levitt's National Football League data show the same direction in a point-spread market. Across 21 seasons from 1980 to 2001 and almost 5,000 games, favourites covered the spread less than half the time, and visiting favourites only 46.7 percent. His 19,770 wagers from 285 bettors in the 2001 season put 68.2 percent of the money on visiting favourites and 56.1 percent on home favourites. Newall and Cortis, reviewing this literature, argue that the direction tracks the number of outcomes. Where a race has many runners, a horse with a win probability above 0.5 almost never exists, so bettors cannot express a preference for near-certainties and the longshot end is where the mispricing lands. Where a contest has two sides, the favourite is a true favourite and the mispricing moves to that end.

study.cite: Snowberg, E., & Wolfers, J. (2010). Explaining the favorite-long shot bias: Is it risk-love or misperceptions? Journal of Political Economy, 118(4), 723-746.

limits: Nothing here is randomised. Odds are equilibrium prices, so the object measured is a market, and the step from a priced curve to a claim about how any person thinks is an inference rather than an observation. Snowberg and Wolfers make the point themselves, writing that the word bias is misleading and that the returns simply falsify a model linear in probabilities and linear in payoffs. The gap in returns is also not a gap anyone can collect. They report that the positive return to extreme favourites suggested by Thaler and Ziemba does not appear in any of their datasets, and Levitt finds little evidence of bettors who systematically beat the bookmaker. Levitt's quantities come from a handicapping contest at one online sportsbook, where entry fees were returned as prize money, so the incentive to pick unpopular sides differs from ordinary betting. Smith, Paton and Vaughan Williams matched bookmaker and Betfair prices for 700 UK races in 2002. They estimated Shin's z, the share of turnover attributable to insiders, at 2.17 percent for mean fixed odds, 1.19 percent for the best available fixed odds and 0.90 percent on the exchange. That is a parameter of an insider-trading model rather than a rate of return, and it says the exchange carries less of the bias, not that the exchange is unbiased. Two papers the brief for this entry named were not obtained. Ali's 1977 estimates and Snyder's 1978 comparison across earlier studies sit behind paywalls at the University of Chicago Press and Wiley. Searches of Crossref, OpenAlex, institutional repositories and the open web during this check found no readable copy of either, so no figure from either appears above. The same applies to Busche and Hall. The bias for lotteries, options and other markets where the term is also used was not examined here.
misreadings: The commonest error is to read the effect as saying longshots lose. They do, and so does every other bet at a track that takes a cut. The claim is comparative and it is about return per unit staked, which is why it needs the whole population of bets at each odds level rather than a tally of winners. A second error is to treat the declining curve as proof that gamblers love risk. Fitted to win bets alone the risk-love and misperception accounts are the same curve, and Snowberg and Wolfers separate them only by pricing compound bets, where misperception wins on all three bet types. Their reading is closer to the probability weighting of prospect theory than to a taste for variance, which is the same machinery behind this site's entries on the certainty effect and probability neglect. Those entries are about choices made by individuals in experiments; this one is about prices, and the agreement between them is a resemblance rather than a shared measurement. A third error is calling the effect a law of gambling. It reverses in baseball, in ice hockey for a period, and in American football spreads, and Snowberg and Wolfers report that Hong Kong and Japanese racing data have not shown it. A fourth is the belief that the last race of the day is worse. That claim rests on small samples from the 1950s to the 1980s, and in Snowberg and Wolfers' data the last-race point estimates differ from the rest by amounts that are not statistically significant.
